Little golden-mantled flying fox (Pteropus pumilus) neonates emerge at a remarkably modest size. Newborn pups weigh approximately 60 grams [Wwb = approximately 60 grams], a value that aligns with allometric predictions based on related congeneric species and the relatively small adult dimensions of this endemic Philippine bat. This initial mass marks the beginning of a developmental period characterized by complete maternal dependency. The onset of nutritional independence, or weaning, occurs at 80 days following birth [tx = 80 days following birth], during which the pup transitions from exclusive milk consumption to foraging for fruit and nectar at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This weaning period, recorded under the typical thermoneutral conditions of the species at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is notably rapid for a pteropodid, reflecting the energetic pressures of a seasonal environment where females must recover body condition quickly between reproductive bouts.

Female little golden-mantled flying foxes reach an ultimate adult mass of 200 grams [Wwi = 200 grams], a figure derived from field measurements of reproductively active individuals in the Visayan Islands. This mass places Pteropus pumilus among the smallest species within its genus. Gestation in this species, by comparison with the better-documented Pteropus rufus, occupies a period of 125 days [tg = 125 days] when measured at the species’ typical active body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This relatively protracted gestation is consistent with the prolonged fetal development observed in other small-bodied island flying foxes, likely an adaptation to ensure that parturition coincides with peaks in fruit availability. Pregnant females substantially increase their food intake during the final trimester, accumulating the lipid reserves necessary to sustain both the developing fetus and the subsequent period of lactation.

Reproductive output in the little golden-mantled flying fox is constrained by the single-offspring rearing strategy typical of the genus. Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], with the majority of adults giving birth to one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year] under the thermal conditions characteristic of their roosting environment at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Some field observations suggest that a secondary litter may occasionally occur when resource availability is exceptionally high, although this appears uncommon. The implications of this low fecundity are profound: population recovery from disturbance is slow, and even modest increases in adult mortality can drive rapid local declines. Conservation strategies for this species must therefore prioritize the protection of adult females, whose reproductive contribution is both limited and indispensable.

Juvenile development proceeds through a distinct series of milestones following the pup’s independence at weaning. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis, is attained at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], which corresponds roughly to the onset of the second breeding season after an individual’s own birth. This delay between weaning and sexual maturation allows young animals to complete skeletal growth and accumulate sufficient fat reserves before entering the highly energetic reproductive arena. Radiotelemetry studies indicate that sub-adults occupy peripheral roosting positions within maternity colonies, presumably reducing intraspecific competition for mates while they continue to refine foraging skills. The prolonged juvenile period, relative to the short weaning duration, suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes future reproductive success over early breeding attempts.

Basal metabolic rate in Pteropus pumilus, measured via respirometry on post-absorptive individuals at rest during their inactive phase, reaches 126.40 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 126.40 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard thermoneutral conditions at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This elevated metabolic expenditure, high for a mammal of this body size, is consistent with the energetic demands of sustained flight and the frugivorous diet that requires frequent feeding bouts. The maximum lifespan recorded for the species extends to approximately 6,278 days [am = approximately 6,278 days], a figure that emerges from mark-recapture studies conducted on the island of Cebu when individuals were maintained at their physiological optimum at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This remarkable longevity, unusual for a 200-gram mammal, underscores a slow pace of life in which low annual reproductive output is offset by an extended reproductive window spanning well over a decade.
